newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HUNGARY'S GKI RESEARCH SEES CPI RISING IN Q2, Q3.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARY'S GKI RESEARCH SEES CPI RISING IN Q2, Q3.

text.p: Hungary's consumer price index (CPI) is likely to rise from quarter to quarter in the next six months, justifying the central bank's surprise rate hike on Monday, GKI Economic Research said on Wednesday.
GKI General Director Andras Vertes told a news conference that energy price rises and seasonal hikes in the prices of agriculture products were likely to boost inflation from March.
"We expect some 19 percent average CPI (of the months) in the first quarter, about 19.2 percent in the second, and it may even reach 20 percent in the third quarter of the year," he said.
Year-on-year inflation was 18.9 percent in January and 18.8 percent in February.

GKI published its economic forecast for 1997 only two days after the National Bank of Hungary's (NBH) 25 basis point hike in the six-month deposit rate to 21.00 percent, and the launching of a 12-month deposit facility at 21 percent.
The NBH said the moves, which shocked a market saturated with repo rate cut expectations, were aimed at protecting savings as market interest rates had fallen too quickly in the past few months.

Vertes said cautious central bank interest rate policies were justified as inflation would probably drop again only in the fourth quarter of this year and a further interest rate decline could threaten real yields on savings.
GKI said that January energy price hikes would appear on the bills from March, and energy prices would continue to boost inflation as they will be adjusted upward later in the year.

Vertes said the planned phasing out of the four percent imports surcharge by July and a cut in the monthly forint devaluation to 1.1 percent on April 1 from 1.2 percent would likely to counterbalance the inflationary impact of energy price hikes.
But the prices of several seasonal agricultural products, which dropped in nominal terms last year, were also likely to rise until September, pushing up CPI figures, he added.
"With average weather and average crop, there will be substantial price rise," Vertes said.
He said the devaluation rate was not likely to be cut further in July, as the government suggested.

The government would probably not want to shock the economy with taking that move in the same time with the abolishment of the imports surcharge, which also weakens the competitiveness of domestic producers, Vertes added.
GKI forecasts a year-on-year CPI of slightly above 18 percent for December, and an 1997 average inflation of 19.5 percent.
Hungary targets ab average inflation of around 17 percent, and the NBH said year-on-year inflation in December was likely to be around also 17 percent.
